sections.why: Scott's premise: a computer is a few very simple parts repeated many times, which is why the lower levels are learnable.
The case for learning how systems work underneath the language you write.
Three concrete reasons understanding compilation pays off: performance, link errors and security.
The hardware a compiled program runs on: buses, memory, processor and the instruction cycle.
How architects frame the same story: performance growth, its sources and its limits.

crossref.mechanism: Work the program asks for that the problem never needed: an interpreter and a slow loop do extra instructions per useful one.

sections.why: A gentle sense of scale: each step is simple, so everything depends on how many steps there are.
Where compilers already remove waste, and what they cannot remove for you.
The translation chain from source to executable, which is where waste is added or removed.
What optimizing compilers can and cannot prove, and why that leaves waste in place.
Amdahl's law: speeding up part of a job is bounded by what remains, which tells you where waste matters.

crossref.mechanism: The C standard leaves some programs undefined; one compiled result is not the language contract.

sections.why: A friendly first example of undefined behavior: reading past the end of an array.

The sanitizer the course uses to catch undefined behavior at run time.
What overflow looks like in the bits, which is exactly the part C chooses not to define for signed types.
Two's-complement addition in hardware wraps; contrast this with C, which leaves signed overflow undefined.

crossref.mechanism: Each .c file is compiled alone into an object file; the linker joins them by symbol name.

sections.why: Compiling separate files to object files and linking them, step by step.

The compile-and-link pipeline from a systems-programming course, with common errors.
What the compiler driver actually runs: preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker.
What static linking does: symbol resolution and relocation.
